en: Preface:
Since the World-Honored One took pity on all sentient beings, he bestowed his transformative teachings according to their capacities.

Among all dharmas, there is none that is more direct, simple, perfect, and sudden than the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land. This [treatise] was therefore composed for the Elder Śāriputra.
It was taught that there is a world in the western direction named Sukhāvatī, where a Buddha resides called Amitābha.
He detailed therein the various adornments of both the environment and its inhabitants, exhorting sentient beings to make vows to be reborn in that land; thus, the teaching of the Pure Land arose.
During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the eminent monk Huiyuan formed a religious society at Mount Lu together with Huiying and Hui...
Holding [the precepts] and so forth—these eighteen individuals collectively cultivated the practices for the Pure Land.
Liu Yimin composed a text on the Vow, while Wang Qiao and others further wrote poems on the *nien-fo sanmei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).

From that time on, the study of the Pure Land was held in equal esteem with the Chan school, and those who followed it increased ever more. Indeed, the poems on the *nien-fo sanmei* by these worthies still circulate to this day.

Biography. I have once read one or two of his works; they merely speak of "the most sublime thought" directing the mind toward the Western Realm, yet they fail to provide a clear and explicit instruction regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. There was a śramaṇa named Fanqi of Siming.
He composed seventy-seven poems titled *Zhùhuái Jìngtǔ* (Meditations on the Pure Land). Among them, he wrote: "Śākyamuni established his teachings in Saṃbhava;
alas, what can be done for sentient beings so turbid and evil? If one wishes to open the secret treasury toward Nirvāṇa, one must follow the Pure Land to point toward Amitābha.
Thus, it is hoped that by breaking through the ford of delusion, one may ascend high to the shore of enlightenment. Nevertheless, these poems of his are merely general remarks.

The general purport is as follows: This work refers specifically to the practice of cultivation. It consists of the Venerable Danyun’s *A Pure Land Life-Saving Boat*, which he himself composed along with his own commentary on the verses. There are forty-eight pieces in total;

each piece consists of four lines of seven characters, while the commentary for each piece ranges from several thousand characters at most to several hundred at least. These works elucidate the meaning of the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations.

He proclaims the principle of unifying phenomena and noumenon within a single mind. Extending this further, he maintains that the Buddha appears from the mind and does not believe there is a Buddha in the West;
he maintains that the Buddha came from the West and does not believe in the manifestation of one’s own mind. Both of these positions constitute false views.

His correct elucidation of the perfect interpenetration of phenomena and noumenon can be described as profoundly penetrating and clearly manifest, most detailed and exhaustive. Yet, its ultimate point of return lies in...

The three gates of faith, aspiration, and practice enable people to know where to begin their work. Furthermore, you have repeatedly emphasized the gains of observing the precepts and the losses of violating them;

your exhortations regarding filial piety and the avoidance of sexual misconduct were particularly earnest and sincere. By following this path to seek the Pure Land, one can truly cross over it with a single reed raft.
As for me, I am by nature of dull faculties and have attained nothing at all regarding the great meaning of the Western transmission; however, I have once...
He annotated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in two fascicles, elucidating the principle that "abiding is itself subduing. His interpretation differed significantly from others.
Upon seeing this, the Master (the recipient) approved of it and requested a preface with a poem. [The author] respectfully recited a verse by Zhi Daolin of the Jin Dynasty, which says:
"The dark ford is remote; a single awakening can serve as a vessel. I vow to [save] all sentient beings submerged in the five [realms]."... [sunk in] the five... [realms].

As for those who are turbid, let us board this ship of great vows together. Written in the sixth month of summer in the twenty-second year of the Guangxu era, when the Jupiter cycle was Róuzhào (Yǐmǎo) and Tōntān (Wùwěi), by the Layman Yú Yuè of Qūyuán in Déquīng.
Short Preface.
I, the unworthy, foolish, and lowly monk Kuānliàng, whose courtesy name is Yuánhǎi, whose style names are Dànyún and Xīduò, am the son of the Yìng family of Yìngxiàn in Sìmíng.
By nature, I am indolent and dull-witted; in my youth, I abandoned poetry and the classics, and upon reaching maturity, I rebelled against the vulgarities of the mundane world.
He did not associate with worldly conditions but yearned only for cool serenity. With joyful heart, he sat cross-legged in silence.
There, he encountered a monastic of the Way and inquired about the wondrous Dharma of non-action. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he resolved to shave his head and don the dyed robes.

Entering the gate of emptiness, he took refuge in the ocean of the Buddhas; receiving full ordination at the renowned monasteries of Mount Taibai and Tiantong, all of which arose from the planting of right causes in past lives, enabling him to experience such sublime retribution.
Rejoicing in his own good fortune, he prayed: "May it be so for me, life after life, birth after birth."
He was profoundly versed in the Confucian classics before leaving the household life to become a monk.

Having fully realized the essence of the mind, he widely proclaimed the True Dharma, causing all who saw or heard him to experience great joy and to receive, uphold, and practice it with faith. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"If one causes sentient beings to give rise to joy, one causes all Tathāgatas to rejoice. Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, by means of their great..."
Because its essence is compassion, one gives rise to great compassion based upon sentient beings; from great compassion, the bodhicitta arises;
and through the bodhicitta, one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment. This is the division of the school at Mount Foding in the Southern Sea, at the practice hall of Huiji of Qiaochuan. I...
In the past, our late teacher, Venerable Juezhao, once remarked: "The primary cause for pure karma is on the verge of being lost and submerged.

All those who harbor this treasure yet remain deluded regarding their own state, turning their backs on the true and heading toward the false, are as numerous as the hairs on a cow. Those who follow such practices are as thick as cow-hair.
Those who possess right view are as rare as the horn of a rhinoceros. This causes those of overweening pride to treat the Way of our Buddha with contempt. How tragic!
The ancient times are distant, and after the long duration of the Dharma, it has fallen into decay. The True Path has become obscured and faint, while false teachings blaze ever more fiercely.
Many people misunderstand and stray onto deviant paths; they do not consider that the single gate of the Pure Land is the shortcut for escaping saṃsāra. Its...

Straight as a bowstring, brilliant as the sun, the profound intent lies within the sutras and śāstras. Failing to encounter an enlightened eye to provide guidance, it is like a group of blind men feeling an elephant;
each speaks of a different aspect, entering darkness from darkness and forever entangled in false views—how truly lamentable!
At that time, [Liang] Zhimù aspired to the vehicle of the ultimate school (zongsheng), yet though he believed, he remained hesitant. He visited Tiantong once more and touched its peak with his head.
He paid his respects before Master Guangyu and requested instruction on the "Sevenfold Investigation of the Mind" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The Master struck him with a single blow right to the head; [Liang] was left bewildered. The Master then further bestowed his compassion, repeatedly providing clarification and instruction. However—
Although his words were repetitive, their meaning was not redundant; he took pity on me with profound kindness and instructed me without weariness.
Subsequently, when the Master retired from the monastery and lived in seclusion at Qingshan Temple on East Lake, I attended him at his side and finally attained realization of the ground.

Thereupon, I traveled to various quarters to investigate the Way, taking up the koan "Who is this that recites the Buddha's name? After investigating it for a long time, I was still unable to reach the state of non-arising.
As for his essential nature, he attained the fragrance of tranquility while simply sitting; within meditative concentration, he experienced nothing but pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
One day, carrying his alms bowl, he came to Hangzhou and dwelt together with the Venerable Jingjue in a thatched cottage at Yuyuan. He frequently studied the sutras and treatises on the Pure Land.
Looking from the present back to the past, those great worthies and supreme sages all unfurled their literary brilliance as a covenant; here, the majestic virtue was vast.
The Confucian [scholar] exhausted his brushwork to compose this vow. From this point on, the dedication of merit shall continue in succession, with chants and responses following one another.
This is truly the great thoroughfare of the Way and Virtue, the direct ferry to eternal bliss.
Therefore, I shall strictly observe my teacher’s command and contemplate only the Six-Syllable Mantra, having no other concerns. He composed a half-verse, saying: "In the mountains, I focus my mind."
The Buddha’s feet do not reach the human realm. Beyond his daily recitations, he constantly and diligently contemplates the meanings clarified in the sutras:
that the great bodhisattvas, by virtue of non-attainment (*anupalambha*), realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Later, upon reading the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he finally understood that "not abandoning" means that within all phenomena there is the power to assist the Path; thus, one does not [cling to them as] receiving [them].

All these are the true mark of dharmas (*dharmatā*), for they are ultimately empty and non-apprehendable. Thus, within the gate of adornment, the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*) remain without deficiency;
within the ocean of True Suchness (*tathatā*), not even a single hair’s breadth is abandoned, because that which is attained is non-attainment.

By treading upon the principle of "attaining the One," one’s doubts are suddenly dispelled. Therefore, Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; Man attains the One...
Thus the Way is accomplished. If one attains ten thousand [teachings], evil is extinguished; if one attains ten thousand [teachings], affairs are concluded.

Considering those base and ordinary people of the present, or late learners from remote corners who do not penetrate the ultimate meaning—those who have long held empty talk in contempt—I recall the ancients and feel dread when thinking of their words, and anxiety when speaking them.
When my thoughts reach this point, shame and remorse arise repeatedly. Therefore, I, a dull-witted person of the Final Dharma...
The fundamental principle is simply to revere single-mindedly the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Therefore, value the substantial over the empty, honor practice over mere discourse, engage with existence without dwelling in existence, and cultivate emptiness without realizing emptiness as a final end. Accumulate extraordinary merit by beginning with even the smallest of virtues.

Relying on a subtle cause, one achieves a great fruit. Tracing back calmly to the period after receiving full ordination at the *caitya*, when his realization had not yet accorded with principle, he then read the various commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Subsequently, setting aside the commentaries, he contemplated the text within stillness and gradually attained insight into the source of the movement and stillness of waves and water, and the principles of the real and false, the empty and substantial. He came to know them.
How great is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*! How sublime is its wondrous function! It serves as the essence of the teaching for the pure hearing-sound of Jambudvīpa;
indeed, it is this very scripture that is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.

I universally pray that those who come after and practice the Way shall first exhaustively investigate the *Śūraṅgama*, and finally return to the single mind of Buddha-recitation. With faith and aspiration supporting one another, they will certainly attain birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, one must strictly purify the *vinaya*; do not covet the reputation of a "hare's horn" nor the sustenance of a "tortoise hair.

This is the most essential point. Having resided in seclusion for a long time, I moved from Yushan to transport earth and timber to Huguosi on White Sand Spring, where I settled for the summer retreat.
There, I carefully read the *Zongjinglu*, the *Weixinjue*, the *Xinfu*, the *Wanshan tonggui*, and other such works by Yongming.
"Even if one has not yet clarified the eye of the Way, one must nonetheless achieve the purification of the body. (Liang) struck the rhythm with sudden clarity and said:
"This ultimately accords with the stage of practice for followers in the末法 (mofa, final age). He then composed a verse: The three karmas are pure and bright, the purified body is accomplished;
All virtues are dedicated to support the pure cause. Those of dull faculties cling to appearances while seeking Bodhi; Through firm faith, vows, and practice, they attain rebirth.

I have often recited these words from my own mouth; through this, my faith and vows have become ever firmer. I hold the Name with constant intimacy, turning the wheel of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) within my oral faculty.
It is like a bell struck by a mallet: the more it is struck, the more it rings; the more it is tapped, the less it can be silenced. Like the wind moving through space, it is unobstructed;
in letting go and gathering back, one attains mastery. Do you not see? It is like the stride of a fragrant elephant crossing a river.
I strode across the torrent. Like a lion crouching on the ground, I repeatedly turned back and cast [obstacles] aside.

Whenever I dwelt in seclusion or sought leisure, whether encountering circumstances that were favorable or adverse, or objects of love or hatred, I invariably made this single phrase of the Buddha’s name my vanguard;
the number of times it has overturned armies and slain generals is beyond reckoning. In the summer of the Xinmao year, my illusory body lost its harmony, and my spirit grew weary.

During his dreams, he beheld red and white lotus flowers, their radiance brilliant and dazzling; suddenly, his breath became calm and his spirit clear, and he single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name, continuing secretly and without ceasing.
In the autumn of the Jiawu year, he moved once again to the Liutong Aranya on South Mountain.

His shadow did not leave the mountain as he made a vow to respectfully transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Once his merit was perfected, he dedicated it toward the nourishment of the lotus roots so they might remain forever firm.
Thereupon, he suddenly forgot his superficial views and exhausted his mental faculties, producing a total of forty-eight poems on the Pure Land.

He extensively searched and widely gathered various sutras and treatises. Among them, he silently identified those that were mutually resonant and in accord with the Pure Land, compiling and annotating them, and entitled the work *The Life-Saving Boat of the Pure Land*.
He himself claimed that by raising the six characters [of the Buddha’s name], he encompassed the boundless ocean of teachings;
by establishing a single principle, he gathered all inexhaustible true expositions. Each point was marked with its essential tenet, and each layer was supported by citations.
I certify that I have universally caused those who sleep amidst the clouds and stand amidst the snow to settle their minds in the Pure Land;

and I have thereby enabled those who investigate principles and explore the profound mysteries to all enter the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanzong*). Therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings, I respectfully compile this collection.

I look up to the Buddha-eye to witness this humble sincerity, and dedicate these merits toward Bodhi, entreating your grace and protection. May all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm ride upon this salvation...

We are born upon the same vessel; together we emerge from the six realms and sink into the bitter sea of saṃsāra, and together we travel through the four lands and the nine grades of the ocean of fruition.

Thus we know that as one ascends the purple-golden terrace, the Original Vow is not in vain; and within the white jade tuft of light, through divine transformation, the single mind rejoices in itself.
May we all together behold Amitābha, together awaken to non-arising, together transform all sentient beings, and together realize wondrous enlightenment.

I was personally ashamed that my own merit and virtue were both so meager, and thus felt it was not yet possible to circulate [this work]. At that time, Mr. Xu Lianchen, a distinguished scholar (xiaolian), said to me:

"I have often heard that medicine has no distinction between noble and base; what cures the illness is what matters. Likewise, the Dharma has no distinction between refined and coarse; what is essential is that which saves the age."

"Why have you kept this secret and not transmitted it? Does the Venerable One harbor a stingy heart regarding the Dharma? (Liang) remained silent and spoke no word. Xu Xiaolian urged him to commit [the text] to woodblocks, saying:

"These forty-eight chapters contain detailed exegesis and commentary. When they meet those with clear vision, they will know for themselves that this is a single piece of sincere and painstaking labor.
If there are those who are crooked, let them be made straight; if there are those who are deviant, let them be set right."

May those who doubt find resolution; may those who are deluded attain awakening. That all people throughout the great earth, within a single thought-moment, may together attain the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance and collectively realize Bodhi—is this not truly magnificent?
Preface written on the day of Dingchou in the second month of spring in the year of Guangxu Bingshen.

While resting at my tomb-chamber by the lakeside, I have repeatedly been honored by your visits, which have opened my heart and mind; my gratitude for this is inexhaustible. Heaven... [The text continues.]
Below, people live in a state of drunken stupor and dream-like oblivion, perversely immersed in profit and desire. Confucianism has been severed, and the Buddha-dharma has likewise declined.
I sought those who study Confucianism but could find none; I sought those who study the Buddha-dharma and found a superior man.
Observing now the "Pure Land Life-Saving Boat" composed by the Honored One above, it penetrates the Buddha-nature to its very depths; how magnificent, how magnificent!
Recorded on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month in the twenty-second year of the Guangxu era by Xia Zhenwu of Fuyang. Preface.
The Great Meaning of the West is expounded in these poetic verses; how could they be mere ordinary words?

In the Pure Realm it is hard to find a raft for transcendence, so with a compassionate heart I have fashioned a life-saving boat. Together we shall travel to the land of Anuttara; there, one personally realizes the sky of emptiness, spirit, and non-obscuration.
I am ashamed that my dull faculties cannot grasp the meaning; even in old age, I remain stuck in the constraints of verbal explanations.

In the winter of the Bingshen year, on the day after the full moon in the tenth month, Yu Yue, the Layman of Qu Yuan, again inscribed this at the Guizhen Chamber of the Xiantai Immortal Lodge on the right side of Nan Shan.
At that time, he was seventy-six years of age.
This is a poem on the Pure Land as a Life-Saving Boat.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Kuānliàng Yuánhǎi of Shànmén in Dìng, Yīn, Sīmíng.

The objective conditions—favorable and adverse, delusion and its midst, the heterodox—are clearly distinguished; one recognizes the original home upon the ground of realization. Thoroughly penetrating, the spring breeze first confers the degree;
before the Buddha, one receives office and has one’s name inscribed upon the Flower Garland.

The five aggregates are the fundamental substance; spirit and mind are most supple and intelligent. Therein lies a Buddha, perfectly still and alert. This alertness within stillness is constantly illuminated;
this stillness within alertness makes the Pure Land serene.

Multitudes of beings emaciated by hunger die and enter the prisons; resolve your will and stand forth valiantly, emulating the heroes of old. To cling to appearances or to become attached to emptiness are both harmful errors;
I urge my fellow practitioners with repeated and earnest exhortation.
The gate of the Sudden Teaching is the single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name; the boundless meanings of the sutras are all subsumed within this source.
Now, as the seal of realization meets the sun setting in the west, I first offer thanks to the Honored One of this Sahā world.
A single formula of one essence surpasses renowned physicians; its efficacy exceeds all others like that of an immortal.
Recite with clear focus on the fixed number in continuous succession; Amitābha is the life-saving boat.
Amitābha flows forth from the very field of one’s own mind; in cultivating the Way, one must further cultivate virtue to its fullness.
When emptiness and existence truly do not obstruct one another, what need is there for a life-saving boat to go or come?
The plum blossoms, amidst the snow, laugh and sing; do not be bound by the five turbidities of this Sahā world. Amitābha, the Compassionate Father, is one’s own original nature;
constantly recite His four characters within the depths of the heart.
Though the myriad phenomena are diverse, they are pruned away in a single thought; the subtle and wondrous Lotus School is the very primal gate.
When the recitation of the Great Name reaches the state of no-mind, one transcends the three realms horizontally, departing and returning at will.
For seven days, maintain the mind without distraction; the roots of goodness and merit will transcend both heaven and earth.
Encompassing the practitioners of the four teachings, this marvel lies solely in being swallowed in one gulp by the person themselves.

Within the realm of both demons and Buddhas, do not speak recklessly; do not pit the Chan school against the Pure Land school. In the original principle of Chan practice, neither birth nor Buddhahood is established;
in the Pure Land, Buddhahood is perfected and realization is certain to come.
One phrase leads, one phrase follows; one sound continues, one sound pursues. Clearly pointing directly, there is fundamentally no duality:
apart from Amitābha, who else could there be?

Born into the Pure Land of Non-birth, this Easy Practice is uniquely sublime and its merit vast. Simply by teaching one to recollect with single-minded devotion, even a child calling out to its mother can escape Saṃsāra.

In a single thought, the adornments of the four lands are perfectly revealed; within the land of non-arising, one’s name is recorded upon the lot. Aversion and delight, relinquishing and grasping, are fundamentally without obstruction;
the Buddha’s words, meeting the capacity of the practitioner, possess a wondrous uniqueness.
Faith, aspiration, and practice—these three are like the legs of a tripod. They are the standard for rebirth and the primary causes and conditions.
Unless one is a "lion cub" who penetrates through the void, one will not truly return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise them without end; in the eastern land, the founding patriarchs paid homage to Master Huiyuan. At Donglin, the lotus-water clock transmits ancient events;
now we hope to inherit the old family tradition.

Ordinary beings bound by all fetters have many karmic obstructions; they must rely entirely on these four characters to transform their inner hearts. The sun of compassion and wisdom can dispel the darkness;
gain and loss truly occur in a single instant.
The ancient tradition of shouting at stones and whipping corpses has long been passed down; yet one's own mind remains bewildered, falling into heterodox paths.
Deluded people fail to recognize this, ensnared by demonic influences, as the Buddha’s teachings decline and the fortunes of the age shift.
The single practice of the six characters encompasses the three gates; the legacy of Shandao endures for a thousand ages.
One must be meticulous regarding the two paths—exclusive and inclusive—to achieve a state of unified focus and behold the Compassionate Honored One.
Those who bear the name of "monk" are not true monks; when have they ever studied the principles of the sutras and shastras?
Making a habit of gluttony their primary concern, they tremble with fear as old age and death approach.
One should maintain the precepts with purity and self-restraint; bodhi is realized by taking the precepts as its foundation. Those who receive them are many, but those who rely upon them are few;
there is no doubt that one who violates them will fall into hell.

From time immemorial, the sin of lewdness is as vast as a mountain; having lost this human body, it is difficult to regain for ten thousand kalpas. One must strictly refrain from foul speech and perverse words;
throughout one's life, remain pure and the mind will be at peace.
Among human virtues, filial piety is foremost; to sever affection and bid farewell to one’s parents is most pitiable. The boundless, profound kindness remains yet unrequited;
may both father and mother board the life-saving vessel together.
The Buddha and sentient beings share the same essential nature. Do not say that eating meat nourishes the spirit; rather, premature death and chronic illness are the retributions for past causes.
Refrain from killing and release living beings to cultivate supreme benevolence.
Who can predict death, birth, old age, and sickness? When the twelve links of dependent origination arise, prepare early for the journey back home;
purify body, speech, and mind to plant the foundation.

Extensively learned and lofty in leisure, he departs from worldly ways; with single-minded right mindfulness, he possesses divine majesty. Refining his person and advancing on the Path, he uses gāthās as medicine;
by practicing according to this, one returns home in the snap of a finger.

Fortune and wisdom should originally be cultivated together; one need only seek them within stillness. With a compassionate heart benefiting all beings and benevolence as the foundation, the fruit of this practice leads back to wandering in the Land of Bliss.
With focused thought and tranquil visualization, the flower of the awakened mind blossoms. A single phrase strikes the vital point, reaching the original home;
through the power of mindfulness, these seven kinds of supreme causes now rescue the aged Danxia.
The wondrous power of Amitābha’s vows is inexhaustible; those who take refuge enter the realm of divine transformation. Like a traveler returning home, one inspects it closely:
flowers bloom in yellow, white, blue, and red.

May the vow to be born in that land be firm and strong; when mindfulness reaches its limit, one realizes emptiness and returns to the native home. At the very moment a thought moves, one is born in the Pure Land;
when the water is clear, the moon appears, revealing the King of the Mind.
One should know that Nāgārjuna’s treatise on the three contemplations is the most excellent; its *udāna* is worthy of praise.
From this point, the place where my mind takes refuge—when my karmic retribution is fulfilled in a future year, may I be nurtured within a lotus flower.

This land is a world of suffering in an age of turbidity; that realm is a lotus paradise of abundant joy. Pointing specifically to environmental conditions for comparison, do not let yourself waste time regarding the fluctuations between high and low, or beauty and ugliness.
With right faith in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, never forgetting one's resolve; the various sutras reveal the radiance of compassion.
Accounts of those who attained rebirth are as numerous as grains of sand, recorded clearly and distinctly in the sacred scriptures.
In this age of the five turbidities, what can one do? Śākyamuni preaches the Dharma to shake off the waves of ignorance.
Now, having realized the source, I return to my home, personally beholding my compassionate Buddha.

The Pure Land originally encompasses both the provisional and the real; to attempt to discuss it as merely provisional is to remain ignorant of the depths of the pearl. Amitābha is no different from the essence of Vairocana;
when ten thousand li are free of clouds, the moon is perfectly full.
Returning home along the road, one steals and kills; within every thought of falsehood, True Suchness is revealed. Seeking birth does not conflict with the dharma of non-arising;
the dharma of arising is entirely subsumed within the mind’s unfolding and rolling up.
The lifespan and radiance are peerless; through the perfect fusion of the Middle Way, one naturally accords with them. Why seek further methods for settling the mind?
For those who practice nianfo, both phenomena and principle are gathered together.

Untainted by worldly toil, his resolve transcends the multitudes. How could one who is not a true companion hear this genuine mechanism? To speak falsely of emptiness while deluded is to be divorced from names;
yet these very names serve as the vanguard that sweeps away the ten-thousand armies.

How wondrous is the loud chanting of the Buddha’s name! Yet the path of "no-thought" is fraught with many divergences. When one attains sudden enlightenment, shards and pebbles become as round as pearls;
the bright moon of autumn shines upon the mountains and rivers.
With all doubts swept away, the three uncertainties are severed; having shattered the four barriers, one maintains firm resolve. Before the end of life arrives, one prepares for death;
those with whom there is affinity assist the Way, their mindfulness mutually supporting one another.
The water of eight virtues flows into the midst of the flowers; reaching this place causes delusive karma to be excised. One is liberated from the cycle of birth and death across billions of kalpas;
such resonance is intimately linked to the power of the Buddha.
Only after awakening does one know that it is precisely here that cultivation is required. The words of the various patriarchs of the various schools are complete and exhaustive.
When a person of full realization chants "Amitābha" from the mouth, they turn back the water-buffalo of Mount Mui.

I have heard that the bliss in the Western Land is exceedingly great; there, the subtle tongue-wheel revolves toward Amitābha. Whether reciting much or little, one must remain in accord with the practice;
each syllable must be distinct and carefully refined.
A single phrase of Amitābha called forth from the mouth; A single orb of bright moon reflects upon West Lake. Now, with one stroke, the message is fully conveyed;
Clapping hands and singing aloud, he is called a true man.

Only when the ground is purified does one know that birth and death are empty. Fully realizing the mind-ground, one attains perfect penetration. Being straightforward and honest, there is no crookedness within;
forgetting both purity and defilement, the two are revealed as mutually interfused.

The Pure Land is easy to realize; its principle is spontaneously perfected. Rebirth therein never deviates from non-arising (*anutpāda*). Saving sentient beings leads to the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
this is the ultimate practice of the eighth stage of non-arising.

The ancients had three methods for earnest exhortation: they carved it into their bones and engraved it upon their flesh, vowing never to forget. Through a hundred refinements and a thousand hammerings, they became iron men;
with noble resolve, they boarded the compassionate vessel.

Everyone should rightly keep Amitābha in mind; nothing is more intimate than self-cultivation. When the original mind is polished until it is like the bright moon, its numinous light takes form within the hollow of a lotus flower.
The sutra text has no characters; the kashaya is white. Shedding blood and carving out my heart, I vow never to abandon it. Dedicate this toward Bodhi and birth in the Pure Land;
may everyone together board the life-saving boat.
